narr: Let's explore the history of Uzbekistan, focusing on the Soviet period and its aftermath.
We'll examine the societal changes, contributions to World War II, intellectual development, resource distribution, and the path to independence.

data.heading: Soviet Repression in Uzbekistan
bullets: Nationalization of property from the rich

narr: During the Soviet era, Uzbekistan experienced significant repression.
The government nationalized property from the rich, targeting the wealthy.
There were four distinct phases of repression that sowed fear throughout society.
These campaigns suppressed alternative thinkers and systematically destroyed national elites.
The first phase occurred in the 1920s to early 1930s.
The second phase was known as 'The Great Terror' from 1936 to 1939.

data.heading: Problem 1 — Contribution to World War II
data.problem: What was the main contribution of the population of Uzbekistan to the Second World War?
data.result: 1,433,230 conscripted (40%+ of able-bodied), 263,005 killed, 132,670 missing, 395,795 not returned, 60,452 invalids; ~120,000 decorated, 280 Heroes of the Soviet Union (75 Uzbeks). Supplied weapons, ammunition, uniforms, food. Hosted 100+ evacuated enterprises and 1+ million evacuees (200,000 children). Opened orphanages and arranged adoptions.

narr: Let's examine Uzbekistan's significant contribution to World War II.
The republic provided substantial military support, with over 1.4 million people conscripted.
This represented more than 40% of the able-bodied population.
Tragically, over 260,000 were killed, with nearly 133,000 missing in action.
Nearly 400,000 did not return from the war, and 60,000 returned as invalids.
Despite these losses, approximately 120,000 were decorated for their service.
Among them were 280 Heroes of the Soviet Union, including 75 Uzbeks.
Beyond military service, Uzbekistan played a crucial role in supplying the front.
They provided weapons, ammunition, uniforms, and food to the war effort.
The republic also housed more than 100 evacuated enterprises.
Additionally, they received over 1 million evacuees, including 200,000 children.
In response to the crisis, orphanages were opened, and many children were adopted by local families.

data.heading: Problem 2 — Intellectual and Scientific Development
data.problem: What was the intellectual and scientific development in the Soviet period?
data.result: Contradictory: literacy grew from 11% to 68% (1928-1939), with 5,504 schools by 1940 and 55,300 specialists by 1941. High poetry, drama, and prose inspired by Jadids (Aibek, Alimjan, Ghulam, Mirtemir, Shaykhzade). Academy of Sciences opened during war due to evacuation of scholars. However, persecution of intelligentsia, alphabet changes, prison terms for Arabic script, ideological contradictions, and destruction of history school (arrest of first history professor, Pulat Saliev).

narr: The Soviet period brought both progress and challenges to intellectual and scientific development in Uzbekistan.
On one hand, there was remarkable educational progress.
Literacy rates increased dramatically from just 11% to 68% between 1928 and 1939.
By 1940, the republic had established 5,504 schools and trained 55,300 specialists.
Culturally, this era saw high poetry, drama, and prose inspired by the Jadids.
Notable figures included Aibek, Alimjan, Gafur Ghulam, Mirtemir, and Shaykhzade.
The Academy of Sciences was opened during the war years, partly due to evacuated scholars.
However, this period was also marked by significant repression of the intelligentsia.
The authorities implemented changes to alphabets and imposed prison terms for using Arabic script.
Ideological contradictions led to the destruction of the history school.
This included the arrest of the first professor of history, Pulat Saliev.

data.heading: Problem 3 — Natural Resources Distribution
data.problem: How were the natural resources of Uzbekistan distributed for the people of Uzbekistan?
data.result: The republic was not the real master of its resources: all revenue from gas, gold and rare metals was controlled by the union center. In the 1980s: gas > 250 billion cubic metres and gold > 50 tonnes annually; minerals worth ~5.5 billion dollars a year. In the last 15 years of the USSR, 'cotton and gold' worth 35+ billion and minerals worth 75+ billion dollars were taken out — while Uzbekistan was criticised for corruption and low productivity. Revenues did not enter the republic's treasury.

narr: Let's examine how Uzbekistan's natural resources were managed during the Soviet period.
A crucial point was that the republic was not the real master of its own resources.
All revenue from gas, gold, and rare metals was controlled by the union center in Moscow.
In the 1980s alone, Uzbekistan produced over 250 billion cubic meters of gas annually.
During the same period, they mined more than 50 tonnes of gold each year.
The total value of minerals extracted was approximately 5.5 billion dollars annually.
In the final 15 years of the USSR, resources worth over 35 billion dollars in 'cotton and gold' were taken out.
Additionally, minerals worth more than 75 billion dollars were extracted during this period.
Despite this wealth extraction, Uzbekistan was criticized for corruption and low productivity.
Crucially, none of these revenues entered the treasury of the republic itself.

data.heading: Problem 4 — Changes During Perestroika
data.problem: What changes took place in the period of perestroika?
data.result: April 1985 — proclamation of perestroika by Gorbachev and 'new thinking'; glasnost weakened ideological control; national movements for sovereignty emerged; demonstrations in 1989 (Fergana, Kokand, Kuvasay, Gulistan, Parkent, Buka); election of I. Karimov as president (March 1990); Uzbek language declared state language (1989); Declaration of Independence (June 1990, 12 articles); GKChP on 19 August 1991 and proclamation of independence on 31 August 1991.

narr: The period of perestroika brought significant changes to Uzbekistan.
In April 1985, Gorbachev proclaimed perestroika and the 'new thinking' approach.
Glasnost weakened the ideological yoke that had constrained Soviet society.
These changes led to the emergence of national movements for sovereignty.
In 1989, demonstrations occurred in several cities including Fergana, Kokand, and others.
In March 1990, I. Karimov was elected as president of Uzbekistan.
Also in 1989, the Uzbek language was declared the state language.
June 1990 saw the Declaration of Independence with 12 articles.
The GKChP attempted coup on August 19, 1991, accelerated the process.
Finally, on August 31, 1991, Uzbekistan proclaimed its independence.

data.title: Weekly Glossary
data.subtitle: Key terms from this week's material

narr: Let's review some key terms that help us understand the history of Uzbekistan during the Soviet period.
These concepts provide important context for the political, social, and economic developments we've discussed.

rows.text: "Soviet man": thinks, behaves and lives only in the Soviet way; the goal of Soviet upbringing
The creation of national republics on the linguistic principle without sovereignty
The New Economic Policy; its curtailment brought back the methods of war communism
Emergency methods of managing the economy of the period of the Civil War
A system of governing society created by the curtailment of the NEP
The forcible unification of dehkan households into kolkhozes; the cause of famine
The confiscation of property and the deportation of "kulaks": 40,000 households (1930–1933)
The one-sided orientation of agriculture to cotton: 93.4% of output by 1937
The creation of industry; in Uzbekistan — predominantly raw-material and agro-technical

narr: Let's examine these key terms that help us understand Uzbekistan's history.
First, 'Homo sovieticus' refers to the 'Soviet man' who thinks, behaves, and lives only in the Soviet way.
This was the ideal promoted through Soviet upbringing and education.
Next, 'nation-building' describes how the Soviets created national republics based on linguistic principles.
Importantly, these republics lacked true sovereignty under Soviet control.
The 'NEP' or New Economic Policy was a more liberal economic approach later reversed.
Its curtailment brought back the strict methods of war communism.
Speaking of which, 'war communism' refers to emergency economic methods used during the Civil War.
The 'bureaucratic command system' emerged from the curtailment of the NEP.
This centralized system governed society through strict control.
Collectivization involved forcibly uniting peasant households into collective farms or kolkhozes.
This policy was a major cause of the devastating famine in the early 1930s.
Dekulakization specifically targeted wealthier peasants, confiscating their property.
Approximately 40,000 households were deported between 1930 and 1933.
Cotton monoculture describes the overemphasis on cotton in agriculture.
By 1937, cotton represented 93.4% of agricultural output in Uzbekistan.
Finally, industrialization in Uzbekistan focused on raw-material and agro-technical industries.
This development served the broader Soviet economy rather than local needs.
